content: The Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020, titled Accelerating towards a leprosy-free world, was developed through extensive consultations with stakeholders, including national leprosy programs, technical agencies, independent experts, public health professionals, funding organizations, and representatives of affected patients and communities. These consultations took place between 2014 and 2015. The strategy is built on three key pillars: (1) strengthening government ownership and partnerships, (2) stopping leprosy and its complications, and (3) eliminating discrimination while promoting inclusion. The primary goal of the strategy is to reduce the global and local burden of leprosy. Specific targets include achieving zero children with leprosy-related disabilities, reducing the number of new patients diagnosed with visible deformities to less than one per million population, and repealing all laws that allow discrimination against individuals affected by leprosy. The strategy was endorsed by the WHO Technical Advisory Group on Leprosy. Since the introduction of multidrug therapy (MDT) three decades ago, the global burden of leprosy has significantly decreased. Leprosaria (leprosy hospitals) were closed, and the disease became manageable at primary healthcare levels. By 2000, leprosy was eliminated as a public health problem globally, and most countries achieved this milestone by 2005. However, achieving subnational elimination in areas with large populations remains a critical challenge. The strategy builds on previous five-year plans, such as the Final Push Strategy (2000–2005), which focused on MDT and passive case detection, and subsequent strategies (2006–2010 and 2011–2015) that emphasized timely detection, effective chemotherapy, and sustainability through integrated services. The current strategy introduces innovative approaches, including increased attention to the human and social aspects of leprosy, reducing stigma, and promoting inclusiveness to enable earlier diagnosis and better outcomes. The strategy also aligns with broader health and development agendas, such as universal health coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 3, which aims to achieve health and well-being for all by 2030. The strategy emphasizes early case detection to prevent disabilities and reduce transmission. It aims for zero disabilities among newly diagnosed children by 2020, achieved through targeted case detection in high-endemic areas, household contact screening, and the introduction of uniform, shorter treatment regimens. The focus on children underscores the unacceptability of leprosy-related disabilities in this population and aims to stimulate community support for the program. Stigma and discrimination remain significant barriers to early diagnosis and treatment completion. These issues negatively impact access to care, treatment outcomes, and the social functioning of affected individuals and their families. The strategy includes specific interventions to address stigma and discrimination, promote social inclusion, and empower individuals affected by leprosy to actively participate in leprosy services. The strategy also encourages national leprosy programs to adapt its principles to their specific contexts, focusing on surveillance and sustaining referral systems. Countries with few or no cases are advised to maintain vigilance through surveillance and linkages with regional centers. The strategy aligns with the WHO roadmap for neglected tropical diseases, which includes consistent targets for reducing grade-2 disabilities (G2D) and integrating leprosy services with other health services. The vision of the strategy is a leprosy-free world, defined as a community free of leprosy-related morbidity, disabilities, and social consequences. By 2020, the strategy aims to achieve zero G2D among pediatric patients, reduce new leprosy cases with G2D to less than one per million population, and eliminate discriminatory laws against individuals affected by leprosy. These efforts will contribute to the long-term goal of eradicating leprosy and its associated challenges.
